headline: NATO foils Russian plot to sabotage undersea cables in Norway with 'secret weapon' training
summary: A joint naval exercise by Britain, Norway, and the U.S. uncovered Russian subs simulating deployment of a secret weapon against critical undersea cables near Norway's Svalbard archipelago.
details: NATO allies reportedly foiled a Russian training exercise simulating the deployment of a secret weapon against undersea cables in Norway. Russian submarines were caught near Norway's Svalbard archipelago, practicing how to disable critical undersea cables without leaving any fingerprints.

The mission to uncover this plot was purportedly a joint naval exercise involving Britain, Norway, and the U.S. While the exercise itself was public knowledge, the revelation of a new weapon, the specific location, and U.S. involvement were previously unknown details.
Norway has two 1,400km cables connecting Svalbard to the mainland, located at a depth of nearly 3km. These cables are among the world's largest and are crucial for relaying satellite data.

The report clarified that the foiled event was a training mission, and no cables were actually damaged during the exercise. The simulation focused on deploying the technology in the event of a conflict with NATO.

No further details were provided about the 'secret weapon' Russia was reportedly using, beyond its design to disable cables without leaving any traces. Russia's GUGI undersea warfare directorate allegedly carried out the operation.

Undersea cables are increasingly viewed as vital infrastructure and potential flashpoints in geopolitical confrontations. Russia has previously been observed loitering over undersea cables in the UK, with one vessel tracking three Russian submarines during a month-long cable survey exercise.

headline_marked: [[US and Mexico team up]] to combat criminal drones with new 'High Eagle' operation
headline: US and Mexico team up to combat criminal drones with new 'High Eagle' operation
summary: The new 'Operation High Eagle' builds on recent anti-drone tech tests along the border, targeting criminal organizations involved in human and drug trafficking. It aims to strengthen cross-border security.
details: The US and Mexico have launched a new collaborative strategy, 'Operation High Eagle' (Águila Alta), to combat drones used by criminal organizations. This initiative builds on recent anti-drone technology tests conducted along their shared border.

The first phase, from August 31 to September 2, involved military forces from both nations simultaneously tracking commercial drones used by criminal entities near San Diego and Tijuana. The second phase, which began September 7 and continues until September 21, focuses on neutralizing these unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) with fixed and mobile anti-drone systems.

While Mexico's Secretariat of National Defense (SEDENA) has not specified the technology, US Northern Command suggests high-energy lasers may be employed. The US Army has invested in systems like the Locust platform, designed to detect, track, and destroy drones from a distance, with prototypes delivered last year.

Mexican authorities have also increased access to advanced anti-drone weapons, signing an agreement with the US Department of Defense to acquire systems at competitive prices. This collaboration aims to strengthen efforts against organized crime, particularly human and drug trafficking.

The US Northern Command reported disabling or destroying approximately 300 criminal drones this year, with a third taken down in August and 11 linked to cartels recently. The operation stems from the US-Mexico Bilateral Implementation Group, ensuring security while respecting national sovereignty.
